I've spent the last three seasons riding from Snowdonia to Skye, and I'm convinced this debate ends more friendships than fuel versus electric ever will. Scotland and Wales both deliver world-class motorcycle touring, but they're fundamentally different beasts—and choosing wrong for your riding style means you'll miss what makes either destination truly magical.

Here's what 15,000 miles across both countries has taught me about where you should point your front wheel in 2026.

The Fundamental Difference: Space vs Intensity

Scotland gives you space. Wales gives you intensity. That's the core truth I've learned after countless trips to both.

In Scotland, particularly once you're north of Perth, you're riding through landscapes that dwarf you. The A82 along Loch Lomond, the A87 to Kyle of Lochalsh, the entire bloody NC500—these routes demand you slow down and absorb the scale. I've ridden the stretch from Tongue to Durness four times, and each time I've stopped at the same viewpoint just to remind myself why I bought a motorcycle in the first place.

Wales doesn't do space. Wales does corners. The A5 through Snowdonia, the A44 from Llangurig to Aberystwyth, the B4391 Bwlch—these roads punch you in the face with corner after corner, elevation change after elevation change. You finish a day in North Wales with your forearms burning and your face aching from grinning inside your helmet.

I love both. But they're not interchangeable, and pretending they are does neither justice.

Roads: Where the Rubber Actually Matters

Scotland's Greatest Hits

The A82 from Glasgow to Fort William is Scotland's calling card. Yes, it gets busy with campervans in summer. Yes, the surface can be sketchy after winter. But riding north with Loch Lomond on your left, then hitting Glen Coe as the mountains close in—it's worth every mile stuck behind a German motorhome. I rate it higher in September when the tourists thin out and you can actually use the throttle.

The A87 to Skye delivers everything the postcards promise. The bridge approach, the Cuillin ridge as backdrop, the twisties through Glen Shiel—I've ridden this route in rain, wind, and (once) brilliant sunshine. Even in the rain it's magnificent. The key is riding it mid-week; weekends bring out every rental car in the Highlands.

The NC500 has become a victim of its own success, but the western section from Ullapool to Durness via the A894 and A838 remains spectacular. I covered this in detail in my complete NC500 guide, but the short version: go clockwise, start early, and fuel up in Ullapool because the next reliable station is 80 miles away.

Lesser-known gem: the B846 from Killin to Bridge of Orchy. Empty, technical, stunning loch views. I've never seen more than three other vehicles on this road. It's part of my Island to Highlands route and consistently surprises riders who've never heard of it.

Wales's Greatest Hits

The A5 through Snowdonia is Wales in concentrate. The Ogwen Valley section between Bethesda and Capel Curig flows like someone designed it specifically for motorcycles. Fast sweepers, clear sightlines, mountain drama on both sides. I've ridden it at dawn to avoid traffic, and at that hour it's religious. The surface is generally excellent—Welsh roads get more maintenance funding than people expect.

The A44 from Llangurig to Aberystwyth crosses the Cambrian Mountains and barely sees a car. This is proper middle-of-nowhere riding, with the kind of third-gear corners that let you feel everything your bike's suspension is doing. The descent into Aberystwyth reveals the sea suddenly, dramatically. Pack layers; it's 10 degrees cooler up top than at sea level.

The A4069 over the Black Mountain (not Black Mountains—different place) is Wales's answer to "but what about proper altitude?" The cattle grid section near the summit rattles your fillings, but the views south toward Swansea and north to the Brecon Beacons are worth it. Go on a clear day or don't bother—mist turns this into a damp, blind slog.

The B4391 Bwlch is famous among riders for good reason. It's short—maybe 15 minutes of riding—but those 15 minutes contain more satisfying bends than some people ride in a month. The northern approach from Llangynog is the one you want. I've watched YouTube videos of people riding this badly, target-fixating into the verge. Learn to look through corners before you attempt it.

After three years of riding both countries extensively, I'd take Scotland for a week-long tour and Wales for a weekend blast. Scotland rewards patience and distance. Wales rewards aggression and skill.

Weather: The Uncomfortable Truth

Both places are wet. Let's not pretend otherwise. But the weather patterns differ in ways that actually matter for planning.

Scotland's weather is changeable. I've experienced four seasons in one ride from Fort William to Skye: sunshine at departure, rain through Glen Shiel, hail at the Skye bridge, then back to sunshine on the island. You pack for everything and you're still caught out. The west coast gets hammered by Atlantic fronts. The east coast (Aberdeenshire, the Borders) is significantly drier but less dramatic scenically.

Wales's weather is more predictable but not necessarily better. The prevailing westerlies dump rain on Snowdonia and the Cambrians consistently. But you can check the forecast with more confidence than in Scotland. If the Met Office says dry, it's usually dry. In Scotland, "dry" means "maybe dry, maybe not, definitely windy."

I've ridden both in September-October, which is my preferred window for both. Scotland gets moodier and more dramatic. Wales gets crisper and clearer. Summer (June-August) brings traffic everywhere, but especially to Scottish Highlands hotspots. May is underrated for both—longer days, fewer tourists, roads recently maintained.

Gear-wise, I don't ride either without proper waterproofs. I've used the same Alpinestars Andes v3 jacket from SportsBikeShop across both countries for two years, and it's handled everything from Skye drizzle to Snowdonia downpours. Don't cheap out on wet weather kit—you'll just be miserable and cut your ride short.

Fuel, Food, and Finding Somewhere to Sleep

Infrastructure Reality Check

Wales wins on convenience. You're rarely more than 30 miles from a petrol station, a decent café, or a town with multiple accommodation options. Even the remote bits (mid-Wales around Elan Valley) have infrastructure within reasonable reach.

Scotland requires more planning. The NC500's western section has genuine fuel deserts. I've stretched my tank beyond comfort between Lochinver and Ullapool because I missed the one station that was open. Small Highland villages might have one B&B that's booked solid in summer. Check ahead, book ahead, or you'll be riding an extra 50 miles for a bed at the end of a long day.

Food is similarly stratified. Wales has decent roadside cafés and pubs throughout. Scotland has excellent food in towns and tourist hubs (Fort William, Portree, Ullapool), but between those hubs you're sometimes choosing between a petrol station sandwich or nothing. I've learned to carry emergency snacks—hitting the Bealach na Bà on low blood sugar is not fun.

Accommodation

Both countries offer everything from wild camping to boutique hotels. I've done the full range—bivvy bag on the Applecross peninsula, luxury B&B in Betws-y-Coed.

For motorcycle-specific hospitality, Wales edges ahead. There are more biker-friendly B&Bs, more cafés that actually understand why you want to park directly outside where you can see your bike, more places that won't make you feel like a nuisance for arriving in textile armour.

Scotland's accommodation can be world-class (some Highland B&Bs are extraordinary), but it's pricier in peak season and booking ahead is essential. Wales is more flexible—you can wing it a bit more, especially mid-week outside school holidays.

Use the VisorUp trip planner to map accommodation options along your route. I wish I'd done this before my first NC500 attempt—I ended up in Ullapool paying £140 for a room I'd have paid £60 for if I'd booked three days earlier.

Difficulty and Rider Experience

Be honest about your skill level. Both destinations can challenge you, but in different ways.

Scotland demands stamina and mental endurance more than technical skill. The distances are long. The weather wears you down. Single-track roads with passing places require different judgment than normal riding. You need to be comfortable with isolation—if something goes wrong on the B869 through Strathnaver, you might wait a while for help.

I'd recommend at least one full touring season under your belt before tackling the remote Highlands. Not because the roads are technically difficult (most aren't), but because you need the experience to handle weather changes, fuel planning, and fatigue management. New riders can absolutely tour Scotland, but stick to the more traveled routes: A82, A87, A9 corridor.

Wales demands technical riding skill more than endurance. The good roads are twisty, cambered, and unforgiving if you get target fixation or brake mid-corner. The B4391, the A4069, the mountain passes through Snowdonia—these aren't beginner roads. But they're shorter. You can ride 150 brilliant miles in North Wales and be back at your accommodation for dinner.

New riders can start with the A5 through Snowdonia (stick to the main route, don't dive onto the B-roads yet) and the coastal A487. Build up to the technical stuff once you're confident with cornering and throttle control.

Scotland vs Wales: Detailed Comparison

Factor Scotland Wales
Best Roads A82, A87, NC500 western section, B846 A5, A44, A4069, B4391, A487 coast road
Scenery Epic scale, mountains, lochs, coastal drama Intense beauty, compact mountain ranges, valleys
Road Quality Variable; excellent on main routes, rough on remote roads Generally excellent; well-maintained throughout
Traffic Heavy on popular routes (A82, NC500), empty on lesser-known roads Moderate; busy on A5 weekends, quiet on mid-Wales routes
Weather Highly changeable, wetter on west coast, windy Wet but more predictable, orographic rainfall on mountains
Distance from England Longer travel time; 6-8 hours from London to Highlands Closer; 4-5 hours from London to North Wales
Fuel/Services Sparse in remote areas; requires planning Good coverage throughout; rarely more than 30 miles between stations
Accommodation Variable; book ahead in season, expensive in tourist hubs Good availability; more biker-friendly options, moderate pricing
Technical Difficulty Moderate; challenges are distance, weather, isolation Higher on best roads; technical corners, elevation changes
Ideal Trip Length 5-7+ days for proper Highland tour 2-4 days for comprehensive North/Mid Wales tour

Pros and Cons Breakdown

Scotland: The Pros

  • Unmatched scale and drama: The landscapes are bigger, wilder, more remote than anything else in Britain
  • Genuine wilderness feeling: You can ride for hours seeing more sheep than people
  • Island hopping: Skye, Mull, Arran—ferry connections add adventure dimension Wales can't match
  • Diverse geography: Highlands, lochs, mountains, coast, glens—massive variety across regions
  • Cultural richness: Distilleries, history, distinct Highland culture adds depth to pure riding
  • The NC500 ecosystem: Like it or not, the infrastructure built around this route benefits all Highland touring
  • Less crowded gems: Once you're off the main routes, you have roads virtually to yourself

Scotland: The Cons

  • Distance from most of England: Getting there eats a full day of riding from southern/central England
  • Weather unpredictability: You can plan meticulously and still get soaked
  • Midges (May-September): Not a riding issue, but stop for five minutes and you'll know about it
  • Infrastructure gaps: Fuel, food, accommodation require more advance planning
  • Tourist traffic on popular routes: A82 and NC500 can be frustrating in peak season
  • Higher costs: Fuel, accommodation, food are all pricier in remote Highlands
  • Single-track road etiquette: Requires learning and patience; not everyone's cup of tea

Wales: The Pros

  • Corner density: More quality bends per mile than almost anywhere in Britain
  • Accessibility: Quick to reach from most of England; you can do a weekend trip realistically
  • Road quality: Consistently well-surfaced and maintained across the country
  • Infrastructure convenience: Easy to find fuel, food, accommodation without extensive planning
  • Compact touring: You can base yourself in one location and ride different routes daily
  • Motorcycle culture: Strong biker community, lots of rider-friendly cafés and accommodation
  • Weather predictability: Easier to plan around forecast; less volatile than Scotland
  • Coast and mountains combo: You can ride mountains in the morning and be seaside by afternoon

Wales: The Cons

  • Smaller scale: It's beautiful, but it doesn't have Scotland's epic grandeur
  • Less wilderness: You're always aware civilization is close; less sense of remoteness
  • Popular roads get busy: A5 on summer weekends, Evo Triangle, Horseshoe Pass—traffic can be heavy
  • Limited route variety: You can exhaust the greatest hits in a long weekend; Scotland offers weeks of unique routes
  • No island options: Anglesey is lovely but it's not Skye
  • Some roads are too technical: If you're not confident with tight corners, Wales can be intimidating
  • Rain shadow effects: West-facing slopes get hammered; you'll ride in rain more often than forecasts suggest

Who Should Choose What?

Choose Scotland If You...

  • Have a week or more to dedicate to touring
  • Value scenery and atmosphere over pure riding intensity
  • Want to genuinely get away from it all
  • Enjoy big miles and long days in the saddle
  • Like combining riding with other activities (distillery visits, hiking, photography)
  • Ride a touring bike, adventure bike, or anything comfortable over distance
  • Don't mind paying premium prices for remote location services
  • Want to include island hopping via ferries
  • Are comfortable with isolation and self-sufficiency

Choose Wales If You...

  • Have a weekend or long weekend available
  • Prioritize technical riding and corner quality over scenery scale
  • Want maximum riding density without extended travel time
  • Prefer infrastructure convenience and flexibility
  • Ride a sports bike, naked, or anything that rewards aggressive cornering
  • Want to improve your technical riding skills
  • Need easier access from central/southern England
  • Prefer to base yourself in one location and do day rides
  • Want more predictable weather for planning

The Best of Both Approach

Here's what I actually do: Wales for weekends, Scotland for annual leave.

I'll hit North Wales four or five times a year for 2-3 day trips. I know the roads well enough now to squeeze maximum riding quality into minimal time. Friday evening ride up, Saturday and Sunday morning blasts through Snowdonia, home Sunday afternoon. It's efficient, satisfying, affordable.

Scotland gets one proper week-long tour per year, usually September. I plan it properly using VisorUp's route builder, book accommodation ahead, and treat it as the year's main motorcycle adventure. The investment of time and money pays off because Scotland rewards that approach.

Trying to do Scotland in a weekend is frustrating—you spend too much time traveling, not enough time experiencing. Trying to stretch Wales into a full week can feel repetitive—you'll ride the same roads multiple times because there simply aren't as many miles of top-tier routes.

My Verdict: It Depends on Your Life, Not Just Your Bike

I'm not giving you a definitive answer because there isn't one. Both are brilliant. Both deserve your time. The right choice depends entirely on your circumstances.

If I could only choose one for the rest of my riding life? Scotland. The variety, scale, and sense of adventure outweigh Wales's corner intensity for me personally. But ask me on a cold February evening when I'm planning my first ride of spring, and I'll be looking at the A5 through Snowdonia because I can be there in four hours and riding proper roads by lunchtime.

Here's my actual recommendation: Ride both. Stop treating it like a binary choice. Wales first, because it's more accessible and forgiving of planning mistakes. Use it to build your touring confidence, understand your bike's limits, figure out what packing strategy works for you. Then take those lessons to Scotland when you've got the time and budget for a proper Highland tour.

The riders who insist one is definitively "better" usually haven't spent serious time in both. I've done the miles. I've made the mistakes in both countries. I've been caught in torrential rain on the A82 and brilliant sunshine on the A4069. I've paid too much for petrol in Durness and found the perfect biker café in Betws-y-Coed.

The real question isn't "Which is better?" It's "Which one matches what I need from motorcycling right now?" Answer that honestly, and you can't go wrong.

Start Planning Your Tour Now

Whichever destination calls to you, start planning properly. Use the VisorUp route builder to map your trip with fuel stops, accommodation, and must-ride roads. Check our detailed route guides for both countries. Get your kit sorted—waterproofs, luggage, phone mount—from reliable suppliers like SportsBikeShop.

And then just go. Stop overthinking it. Stop waiting for perfect weather that never comes. Both Scotland and Wales are waiting with roads that'll remind you why you started riding in the first place.

See you out there.

—Jack
